checks: The local Lipschitz property of F follows by composing the two locally Lipschitz maps. The classical first derivative of g=V∘q gives ∇g=(Dq)ᵀF, a locally Lipschitz gradient because q is C² and its derivative and F are locally bounded.

The weak Hessian is symmetric by commuting distributional derivatives of g. At almost every point Rademacher and the ordinary product rule identify it with (Dq)ᵀDF+Σ_a F_a D²q_a, and the latter sum is symmetric. No differentiability of ∇V at q(y) is needed.

At any point of differentiability of F, convex gradient monotonicity yields a nonnegative difference scalar product along y+tv; openness permits both directions for small t. Division by t² gives the quadratic-form inequality for every v at that same point. Together with symmetry this is positive semidefiniteness.
An exact check of the singular-image case is V(x₁,x₂)=(x₁²+max(x₂,0)²)/2 and q(y)=(y,0): ∇V is not differentiable on the image, but F(y)=(y,0) and the pullback matrix is the scalar 1.

summary: The derivative and symmetry argument is intrinsic to the parameter domain, so it applies even to a q-image contained in the ambient nondifferentiability set of ∇V.
